Is it public knowledge that European and U.S. plugs for Supercharger stations are different?

Yep. Tesla drivers also carry a bunch of adapters for other standards. There's a CHAdeMO to Tesla adapter so they can use the 50kW charge stations for example. All Teslas outside the US are different. It is one of the joys of having an EV - you have to carry adapters. I have a LEAF which is one of the best supported so I can directly use the CHAdeMO chargers without an adapter (20 mins to 80% charge), and also the J1772 cables which are usually 15A (8 hours to charge) or 30A (4 hours to charge.) Plus, I carry an 8A EVSE which can be plugged into any wall socket although it is really slow (16 hours to charge) and have a 15A Commando socket on a separate circuit in my garage with a 15A EVSE on that which will get my car to full in 8 hours. Lastly, I have a Menenkes type 2 adapter cable which plugs into a european style socket and has a J1772 that plugs into my car (I have a 6.6kW onboard charger so 4 hours to charge on one of those) but I have yet to encounter one so I don't carry it with me. Most charging stations have appropriate cables attached for my car anyway since it is the most common EV on the roads here. It's a real mess out there.
Thanks for the rundown, I had no idea that charging connectors were so fragmented! (Although in hindsight I should have expected it, every other damn type of connector comes in a million variants.)

Yep. Just look at USB :-)

The good news with charging EVs is the actual standards of the protocols are generally common so you just need an adapter depending on your car. I would still be wary of buying a car that is rare or unusual in some way. There's lots of interest here in the Renault Zoe because it seems better able to handle hills than the LEAF does but it doesn't have a CHAdeMO socket, just a 63A AC Menenkes by the look of it and since most chargers that can use are only 30A (7kW) at most, then that puts a serious limitation on the car because although it can go 200Km a charge, it will then take you around 4 hours to charge it up again to go further. My LEAF can do around 130-160Km depending on speed and terrain but I can charge up to 80% in 20 mins and be off again so long distance runs are much more practical if there are fast chargers.
